title: Compatibility playbook for OpenAI Responses mapping and runtime trade-offs
creator: Ava Martinez
body:
Purpose:
This ticket captures a practical engineering playbook for mapping OpenAI Responses API semantics onto Redwood's Core API surface, calling out concrete parity gaps, runtime trade-offs, and an executable phased rollout plan. The intent is to provide a repeatable mapping layer we can ship behind a feature flag that preserves Redwood runtime guarantees (latency SLOs, KV cache correctness, safe fallbacks) while aiming for high behavioral compatibility for customers migrating integrations or using third-party SDKs.

Scope and non-goals:
- In scope: streaming event mapping, tool/function calling behavior, structured output encoding (including partial/invalid json handling), prompt/message role semantics, top-level metadata, and canonical error mapping.
- Out of scope: model weight-level optimizations, customer billing changes, and UI changes in Console (Console follow-up ticket will be created for surfacing compat flags).

Summary of parity gaps observed so far (high level):
1) Streaming event envelope differences: OpenAI uses "event" style streaming chunks with types like "response.delta", "response.created", "response.error". Redwood currently streams raw tokens via chunk frames and implicit end-of-stream markers. We need a deterministic envelope so 3rd-party SDKs expecting ResponseEvents can interop.
2) Function/tool calling wire format: OpenAI allows both explicit function_call objects and inferred behaviors where the model emits a special assistant message with name and arguments; our current function calling plumbing uses a different signal (tool invocation topic + separate invocation channel). Edge cases include multi-turn tool returns and nested tool calls.
3) Structured output validation and partial JSON: OpenAI tolerates partial JSON fragments over the stream which clients may buffer and attempt to parse; Redwood's runtime may pre-tokenize or perform detokenization that changes chunk boundaries and makes client-side incremental parsing brittle.
4) Metadata and annotations: OpenAI Responses attach metadata like "warnings", "content_filtering", and safety labels. Redwood has similar constructs but different key names and placement (per-token vs per-response).
5) Resume/retry semantics: when clients reconnect mid-stream, OpenAI provides deterministic checkpoints via "response.id" and sequence IDs. Redwood currently lacks sequence IDs in streaming frames.

Recommendations and mapping rules (concrete):
- Streaming envelope: implement an optional event wrapper layer that can be toggled per-route. When enabled, every token/frame will be emitted as a JSON event with a stable set of fields: {"type","response_id","cursor","delta","role","timestamp"}. This avoids changing core runtime tokenization while offering compatibility. The wrapper will be opaque in the runtime (no reassembly) and implemented as a small middleware in the gateway layer.
- Response IDs and cursors: augment the stream with a UUID response_id and a monotonically increasing cursor integer. These fields must be included in both streaming and the final non-stream response for consistency. This enables resume semantics.
- Function calling: map OpenAI function_call to Redwood tool invocations by translating the OpenAI function_call.name -> Redwood tool_id and function_call.arguments -> tool_input JSON. For streaming function calls, emit a specific event type "tool.invoke.delta" and ensure the final tool result is delivered as a distinct "tool.result" event with an explicit content_schema field. Support for multi-tool sequences must be explicit: include a parent_tool_id on tool.result for nesting.
- Structured output and partial JSON: do not change tokenization. Instead, provide a streaming header that annotates chunk byte offsets alongside token deltas so client SDKs can safely reassemble JSON across frames. Add an optional header flag "structured_streaming=v1" and document reassembly algorithm in the SDK migration guide.
- Error mapping: map OpenAI numeric error codes and strings to Redwood equivalents at the gateway; preserve original error text in a metadata field "compat.original_message" for observability.

Runtime trade-offs considered: 
- Adding envelope metadata increases per-frame size and CPU for serialization. To mitigate, the envelope layer will be applied only for compat routes and will use compact JSON (no whitespace), and binary protocols will be considered in a subsequent perf spike.
- Providing response_id and cursor improves resume semantics but requires idempotency guarantees in gateway; we will implement lightweight in-memory windowed checkpoints for canaries, and persist only on rollback or failure.
- Tool invocation semantics add bookkeeping for nested tool_ids. This increases stateful tracking across a request lifecycle; we will bound this by limiting nesting depth to 3 for the initial release.

Testing and canary plan:
1) Unit tests: mapping layer conversion tests for 50+ edge cases (partial JSON fragments, multi-tool responses, reconnect sequences).
2) Integration tests: end-to-end with sample OpenAI SDKs (node/python) that expect Responses API semantics. Test both streaming and non-streaming flows.
3) Load test: run a compat-enabled gateway pool at 5% production traffic with synthetic users to measure P50/P95 token latencies and CPU overhead. Goal: less than 12% P95 latency regression.
4) Canary rollout: 1% -> 5% -> 20% -> 100% with automated dead-man switch if error-rate > 1% or latency regression > 25% at any step.

Telemetry additions:
- counters: compat.stream.enabled, compat.tool.invocations, compat.resume_attempts
- histograms: compat.stream.frame_size_bytes, compat.stream.serialize_ns
- traces: annotate gateway -> runtime spans with compat=true tag and include response_id and cursor.

Migration notes for customers and SDKs:
- Document header: how to enable compat mode per-route and per-api-key.
- SDK helper: provide a compatibility module that replays OpenAI-style events into existing SDK consumers (node/python).
- Migration checklist: enable feature flag, run integration tests, verify reconnect/resume behavior, test function-call tool mappings.

Open questions and outstanding risks (requires design review):
- Should the envelope be plain JSON or a lightweight binary TLV? Binary reduces size but increases client SDK complexity.
- Do we persist response_id/cursor to durable storage for long-running responses or rely on ephemeral gateway state?
- Edge case: models that emit function call names not present in the customer's tool registry. Proposed mitigation: emit a synthetic tool stub event and set tool.result to an error with reason="unknown_tool".

Progress updates and recent activity:
- 2025-02-10: Ticket created with initial gap analysis.
- 2025-02-18: Spike completed to prototype envelope middleware and measure overhead on a single 8xA100 gateway. Measured ~7% CPU increase at 95th percentile token throughput. Artifact: docs/spikes/compat-envelope-2025-02-18.md (see artifacts list).
- 2025-02-24: Internal design review with PM and Runtime leads. Decision: initial release will be JSON envelope with response_id/cursor, no binary TLV for MVP. Action: add canary checks and telemetry.
- 2025-03-01: Implemented gateway-side serializer and unit tests. PR opened: https://github.com/redwood-inference/redwood/pull/4123
- 2025-03-04: Integration tests failing intermittently when streaming partial JSON; root cause appears to be client buffering assumptions. Added reassembly offsets to envelope and updated SDK reassembly algorithm. PR updated: https://github.com/redwood-inference/redwood/pull/4123

Next steps (short term):
- Finish integration test harness that runs upstream OpenAI SDKs against compat gateway (owner: Liam).
- Add histogram telemetry and canary automation (owner: Priya S.).
- Draft customer migration guide and SDK compat helper (owner: DOCS team, ticket to be created).
- Schedule security review if binary TLV option is considered in future.

Acceptance criteria:
- Compat mode produces event streams that OpenAI SDKs can consume without code changes for at least 90% of our test cases.
- Streaming P95 latency regression < 12% when compat mode enabled under synthetic load.
- Function calling mapping supports nested tool calls up to depth 3 and surfaces unknown-tools with predictable error events.
- Resume semantics allow reconnect+resume for 95% of reconnect scenarios in integration tests.

Longer-term items (future tickets):
- Evaluate binary TLV to reduce envelope overhead.
- Add persisted response checkpoints for very long-running streams.
- Console UX: surface compat mode per-route and show compat metrics in per-route dashboard.
